exercises.title: True and False
exercises.content: Python has a special type called a boolean — it can only be True or False (with capital letters!). Comparisons always give you a boolean result. These are the foundation for making decisions in code.
exercises.code:
print(True)
print(False)
print(type(True))

is_raining = False
print(is_raining)

highlights.note: True and False are special Python values — always capitalized!
You can store True/False in variables too — great for on/off flags.

exercises.title: Watch: Boolean Variables
exercises.code:
sunny = True
hot = False
print(sunny)
print(hot)

exercises.title: Equal and Not Equal
exercises.content: Use == to check if two values are equal. Use != to check if they are NOT equal. Important: = assigns a value, == checks equality — they're different! The result is always True or False.

highlights.note: == asks 'are these equal?' — 5 == 5 is True, 5 == 3 is False.
!= asks 'are these NOT equal?' — 5 != 3 is True (they're different).
== works on strings too! "cat" == "cat" is True, "cat" == "dog" is False.

exercises.title: Watch: Equal Comparisons
exercises.code:
x = 10
y = 10
result = x == y
print(result)
y = 5
result = x == y
print(result)

exercises.question: Create two variables: x = 5 and y = 10. Print whether they are equal (use ==).

exercises.title: Greater Than and Less Than
exercises.content: Use > (greater than) and < (less than) to compare which value is bigger or smaller. These work on numbers and give you True or False.

highlights.note: 3 > 8 is False — 3 is NOT greater than 8.
9 < 4 is False — 9 is NOT less than 4.

exercises.title: Watch: Greater/Less Than
exercises.code:
score = 85
passing = 70
result = score > passing
print(result)
result = score < passing
print(result)

exercises.title: Greater/Less Than or Equal To
exercises.content: Use >= (greater than or equal to) and <= (less than or equal to) when you want to include the equal case. The key difference: 5 > 5 is False, but 5 >= 5 is True!

highlights.note: 5 is NOT greater than 5 (False), but it IS greater than OR equal to 5 (True).
3 is NOT less than 3 (False), but it IS less than OR equal to 3 (True).

exercises.title: Watch: Boundary Comparisons
exercises.code:
age = 18
min_age = 18
print(age > min_age)
print(age >= min_age)
print(age < min_age)
print(age <= min_age)

exercises.question: Create variables 'temperature' = 100 and 'boiling' = 100. Print whether temperature is greater than or equal to boiling.

codeTests.message: Compare temperature >= boiling (using the variable names)

exercises.title: Comparing with Variables
exercises.content: You can store comparison results in variables — they become True or False. This is useful for making your code more readable by giving names to conditions.
exercises.code:
age = 15
is_teen = age >= 13 and age <= 19
print(is_teen)

score = 95
is_perfect = score == 100
print(is_perfect)

highlights.note: Store the comparison result in a descriptive variable name — makes code easier to read!
is_perfect will be True only if score is exactly 100.

exercises.title: Watch: Stored Comparisons
exercises.code:

price = 50
can_afford = price <= budget
print(can_afford)
